LanguageData.OrganHypoxia.label: hypoxia
LanguageData.OrganHypoxia.description: Insufficient oxygen supply to this part of the body has caused cells to start metabolizing anaerobically, leading to the production of lactic acid and acidosis, and to eventually die, causing tissue damage. If the underlying cause of the hypoxia is not immediately treated, the affected tissue will continue to deteriorate, eventually leading to multiple organ failure and death.\n\nWith delayed vital failure enabled, ongoing systemic oxygen deprivation prevents ordinary healing of this injury. Restoring circulation and breathing permits normal recovery.
LanguageData.BrainDamage_Hypoxia.label: cerebral hypoxia
LanguageData.BrainDamage_Hypoxia.description: Prolonged lack of oxygen to the brain has caused neurological damage. Depending on the severity and duration of the hypoxia, damaged cells may be able to recover, or they may die off and cause permanent brain damage and disability. Restore oxygen delivery promptly; surviving tissue may recover, while lasting disabilities need separate care.\n\nWith delayed vital failure enabled, sustained oxygen deprivation steadily adds cerebral injury, with some variation in its pace. Complete deprivation can become fatal in approximately 1.5 game hours; the final cerebral injury stage is terminal. Injury amounts scale with the affected brain, preserving comparable physiological rescue windows across body sizes. Artificial coma halves new hypoxic brain injury, but does not restore oxygen delivery or stop organ-failure timers. Treating the injury cannot replace oxygen delivery. After circulation and breathing recover, ordinary injury healing resumes, while lasting neurological disabilities may remain. With neurological damage enabled, worsening injury guarantees increasing lasting consequences at clinical milestones, beginning at 5% of the affected brain's maximum health.
